name: God's knowledge of particulars
plain_explanation: If God only knows general truths and universals, not this particular person or event, that seems to threaten the Christian doctrine of Providence (which requires God to know and care about individual lives). But there are serious objections: particulars are made of 'signate matter,' which an immaterial being seemingly cannot know; particulars come in and out of existence, which seems incompatible with the unchanging character of divine knowledge; some particulars are contingent, not necessary, so it seems they cannot be certainly known in advance; and particulars are infinite in number, seemingly beyond any finite grasp. Aquinas answers that God knows particulars as their cause (much as a maker knows what he is making), that God sees all times as an eternal present rather than in temporal sequence, that He knows our minds directly, and that nothing is truly 'trivial' since the order of the universe as a whole is noble and cannot be known without knowing its parts.
precise_definition: Aquinas's resolution, in Book I of the Summa contra Gentiles, of seven objections to the claim that God has knowledge of individual, contingent, and even seemingly trivial or evil particulars, arguing that God's causal, atemporal mode of knowing avoids all seven difficulties.
why_it_mattered: This question, which Russell notes 'had already troubled both Plato and Aristotle,' is essential to reconciling divine omniscience with Christian Providence, free will, and the moral significance of individual human lives.
historical_origin: Treated systematically by Aquinas in Summa contra Gentiles, Book I.
examples: The seven objections Aquinas enumerates and then answers, including that singulars are 'too petty for God's attention' and that 'in some singulars there is evil, but God cannot know evil'
Aquinas's reply that God knows evil because knowing any good involves knowing its opposite
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly grounds the Christian doctrine of Providence.
